title: Stack: build it three ways, then use the STL
overview: A stack is Last-In-First-Out: the last value you push is the first one you get back. This module builds a stack class on top of a `vector`, a hand-made doubly linked list and the STL `list`, then shows the ready-made `stack<int>`. It also starts a queue on a singly linked list. The goal is to see that the same five operations — push, pop, top, size, empty — can sit on different storage, all in O(1).

concepts.explain: Think of a pile of plates: you add to the top and take from the top. Values come out in the reverse of the order they went in.
`push(x)` adds on top, `pop()` removes the top, `top()` reads it, `size()` counts, `empty()` tells if nothing is left. All are O(1).
The back of the vector is the top: `push_back`, `pop_back` and `back()` do all the work.
Keep a `tail` pointer and treat the tail as the top. With a doubly linked list, `pop` can step back with `tail->prev` in O(1).
Calling `top()` or `pop()` on an empty stack is undefined behaviour (often a crash). Always guard: `while(!st.empty())`.
A queue adds at the tail and removes from the head, so the first value in is the first out. A singly linked list with `head` and `tail` pointers gives O(1) for both.
A class cannot have a data member and a member function with the same name. `int size = 0;` plus `int size()` is a compile error — rename the counter (for example `sz`).

files.title: Stack class on a vector (fixed values)
files.what: Builds `myStack` on a `vector<int>` and exercises push, pop, top and empty with hard-coded values.
steps: `push` → `v.push_back(val)`; `pop` → `v.pop_back()`; `top` → `v.back()`.
`size` and `empty` just forward to the vector.
`main` pushes 10..60, prints the top (`60`), pops, prints the new top (`50`).
It prints the top again after checking `empty()`, then prints-and-pops once more.
Finally it empties the stack in a `while(!s.empty())` loop, printing each top.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.output_note: `60`, then `50` three times (top shown twice without popping, then printed and popped), then `40 30 20 10` — the remaining values come out newest first.

check.q: Why is the end of the vector used as the top, not the front?
check.a: Adding/removing at the back is O(1); at the front every element would have to shift, O(n).

files.title: Vector stack with input
files.what: Same vector-based `myStack`, but the values are read from input and then printed by popping until empty.
steps: Read `n`, then push `n` values.
While the stack is not empty, print `top()` and `pop()`.
files.output_note: `7`, `6`, `5` on separate lines — the reverse of the input order.

files.title: Stack on a doubly linked list (does not compile)
files.what: Builds `myStack` from `Node`s with `next` and `prev`; the tail is the top.
steps: `push`: create a node; if the list is empty it becomes both `head` and `tail`, otherwise link it after `tail` and move `tail`.
`pop`: remember `tail`, step `tail = tail->prev`, delete the old node.
If `tail` became `NULL`, the stack is empty, so set `head = NULL` too; otherwise cut `tail->next`.
`top` returns `tail->val`; `size` counts pushes minus pops.
`main` reads `n` values and prints them by popping.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.output_note: No output: the file fails to compile. Once fixed it would print `40 30 20 10`, one per line.
files.watch_out: Compile error: the class has both `int size = 0;` and `int size()`. Fix: rename the counter to `sz` (as done later in Module 14's `practice_problem_1_same_stacks.cpp`).

check.a: After removing the tail, the stack must find the new tail in O(1); `tail->prev` gives it directly. A singly linked list would need a full walk.

files.title: DLL stack (practice copy, same compile error)
files.what: Re-typed copy of the doubly linked list stack; the object is named `st`.
steps: Same `push`/`pop`/`top` logic; the loop uses `!st.empty()`.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.output_note: No output: same compile error as the original.
files.watch_out: Same clash between `int size` and `int size()`; rename the member to `sz`.

check.q: After pushing 7, 8, 9 and popping once, what are `head->val` and `tail->val`?

files.title: Stack on the STL list
files.what: `myStack` stores values in `list<int>` (a doubly linked list inside) and uses its back as the top.
steps: `push` → `l.push_back`, `pop` → `l.pop_back`, `top` → `l.back()`.
`size` → `l.size()`, `empty` → `l.empty()`.
`main` reads `n` values and pops them all, printing each.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)

check.q: Which `list` function removes the top in this design?

files.title: STL `stack<int>`
files.what: Uses the built-in `stack<int>`: five values are pushed in code, more are read from input, then everything is popped and printed.
steps: Push `10 20 30 40 50` directly.
Read `n` and push `n` more values on top.
`while(!s.empty())` print `s.top()` then `s.pop()`.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input_note: `n`, then `n` values that go on top of the five built-in ones.
files.output_note: `70 60 50 40 30 20 10`, one per line: the input values come out first because they were pushed last.
files.watch_out: `s.pop()` returns nothing (`void`); read `s.top()` first if you need the value.

check.a: Nothing — it is `void`. Use `top()` to read the value before popping.

files.title: Queue on a singly linked list (first try, does not compile)
files.what: Starts a `myQueue` class: push at the `tail`, pop from the `head`, so values leave in the order they came in.
steps: `push`: link a new node after `tail` (or make it `head` and `tail` if empty).
`pop`: delete `head` and move `head` forward; if the queue became empty, reset `tail` to `NULL`.
`front` reads `head->val`, `back` reads `tail->val`.
`main` only reads `n` values and pushes them; nothing is printed yet.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.output_note: No output: the file fails to compile (and `main` prints nothing even when fixed). The finished version is in Module 14.
files.watch_out: Two mistakes: `int size` clashes with `int size()` (rename the counter), and the `Node` constructor does `this->next = next;` which copies the uninitialised member onto itself — it should be `this->next = NULL;`.

check.q: Why must `pop` set `tail = NULL` when the last node is removed?
check.a: Otherwise `tail` still points to deleted memory, and the next `push` would write through that dangling pointer.

recap: push / pop / top / size / empty are all O(1) on vector, linked list or STL.
The 'top' is the end where you can add and remove cheaply (vector back, list tail).
A class member variable and method cannot share a name.

check_yourself.q: You push 1, 2, 3 and pop twice. What is on top?
Why is a vector a poor base for a queue but fine for a stack?
check_yourself.a: A queue removes from the front, which is O(n) in a vector; a stack only touches the back, which is O(1).

check_yourself.q: In the doubly linked list stack, what two pointers must be fixed when the last node is popped?
check_yourself.a: `tail` becomes `NULL` and `head` must also be set to `NULL`.
